A leased horse became unsound. Who pays?

An unsound leased horse is a horse whose condition may prevent the use agreed in the lease. Who pays is a separate question from who owns it: the lease may distinguish routine care, emergency treatment, insurance and loss of use. Start with the condition’s timing and the actual expense clauses, rather than assigning every bill to one party.

Publisher: Wise Covington PLLC · Updated 2026-11-03

Which records separate treatment from payment responsibility?

Keep the horse’s immediate care separate from the disagreement over reimbursement. Record the veterinary findings, when signs first appeared, who noticed them and who authorized treatment. A condition discovered during a lease is not, by itself, a complete explanation of when or why it arose.

Which facts need to be compared?

Question to resolveRecord to check
Before the leaseCollect the condition report, examination and any disclosed limitations.
At the first signPreserve dated observations and the veterinary assessment.
When care was authorizedIdentify the decision maker, notice given and expense clause.
If riding stopsCheck loss-of-use, termination, transport and insurance provisions separately.

Read routine-care and emergency-care provisions separately. Identify any limits on treatment authority, the agreed notification route and any instruction about consulting the owner. Compare those terms with what actually happened, including messages and invoices.

Look for provisions addressing an unusable horse, suspension of payments, return transport and early termination. A clause assigning veterinary bills does not necessarily answer whether the lease continues. Avoid treating a payment dispute as permission to abandon the horse or stop necessary care.

Does insurance decide who owes the veterinary bill?

An insurance policy and a lease answer different questions. Check the policy’s insured parties, reporting conditions and coverage terms alongside the lease’s expense allocation. An expected claim payment is not proof that a particular bill is covered or that the parties agreed who carries an uninsured balance.
